newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan land prices drop for fifth consecutive year.
newsitem.headline: Japan land prices drop for fifth consecutive year.

text.p: Japanese land prices dropped almost eight percent on average in 1996, falling for the fifth consecutive year, the government said on Monday.
It added that not all the news on the property front was bad, however, as the rate of the price decline slowed compared with the hefty losses of the previous four years.
The National Tax Administration said the price of one square metre (yard) of land in urban areas averaged 176,000 yen ($1,504) nationwide in 1996, down from 192,000 yen ($1,641) a year earlier.

But even with the latest drop, land in Ginza, Japan's most expensive shopping and office district in central Tokyo, still cost 11.36 million yen ($97,094) per square metre, down a more modest 5.3 percent from a year earlier.

In the five years prior to 1991, Tokyo property prices soared by 170 percent, fuelling a "bubble" economy of inflated asset prices. Property prices peaked out and started plummeting in 1992 after the collapse of the bubble.
Including the eight percent drop in 1996, Japan's land prices have fallen by more than half from their peak levels in 1992, according to official statistics.
By region, the price of land in Tokyo dropped 11 percent in 1996 to an average 584,000 yen ($4,991) per square metre, while land prices in Osaka, western Japan, fell by 9.5 percent.
Property analysts said that residential land prices in major cities in Japan are almost stable now, although prices of land for commercial use are still falling.

"In general, prices of residential land have stopped falling and are now levelling off... But the outlook for the land market is still uncertain," said Takeshi Fukuzawa, president of Mitsubishi Estate Co, Japan's leading real estate firm.
Analysts said lots in commercially attractive areas are being traded actively, although there is little trade in other types of land.
An official at the National Land Agency said earlier this month that the pace of the decline in commercial land prices in major urban areas should continue to slow. ($1=117 yen)
